senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀβαρής ‘to be light in weight,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to not being financially burdensome to anyone
land under cultivation or used for pasture

senses.subdomain: Areas Which Are Uninhabited or Only Sparsely Populated
senses.def: a rural area in contrast with a population center
senses.comment: A rural area is often identified by a term or phrase meaning ‘extension of fields’ or ‘place of field after field’ or ‘area of farms.’

senses.def: a relatively small village, possibly merely a cluster of farms
to experience or suffer a loss of blood

six-legged winged insect characterized by the fact that its third pair of legs is elongated and adapted to hopping; Acrididae family; moves in swarms that migrate to new areas, which they colonize; at other times lives solitary or in small groups; eaten cooked by toasting, grilling, frying, or broiling, though in some places they are also eaten raw; because of their large numbers and swarming characteristics, locusts were a symbol of a vast attacking army against which there was no defense and also a symbol of divine punishment
senses.comment: The four NT contexts in which ἀκρίς occurs refer to these insects either as being edible (Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6) or as being very destructive (Revelation 9:3).|Some persons have assumed that the reference to grasshoppers being eaten by John the Baptist should be understood not as the insects but as carob pods, but there is neither linguistic nor cultural evidence to support such an interpretation.|In a number of parts of the world there are different kinds of grasshoppers/locusts, some of which are edible, and others which are not edible. It is therefore important in the contexts of Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6 to select a term which designates edible insects.

senses.def: pertaining to not losing the wonderful, pristine character of something
to make known that which has presumably been hidden or unknown previously

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
to come back to life after having once died
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a difficulty involved in formulating some expression for ‘resurrection’ or ‘living again,’ since such a phrase may refer to what is technically known as metempsychosis, that is to say, the rebirth of the soul in another existence, a belief which is widely held in a number of areas of south Asia. This problem may be avoided in some languages by speaking of ‘his body will live again’ or ‘his body will come back to life’ or ‘he will be the same person when he lives again.’|One may also translate ‘there is no resurrection’ as ‘people will not live again.’

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a process of change from a lower to a higher status (note the contrast with πτῶσις[b] ‘a falling,’ 87.75)
senses.comment: ἀνάστασις in Luke 2:34 may also be interpreted merely as a change for the better (see 13.60).|Reversals of rank and status are a frequent theme in the declaration of the prophets, and this becomes particularly significant in the Magnificat (see Luke 1:46).

senses.def: a change for the better
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀνάστασις in Luke 2:34, see 87.39.

senses.def: a prophetess
pertaining to that which cannot be seen
senses.comment: See translation note at 24.3.

senses.def: to cause something to be known as genuine, with possible focus upon the source of such knowledge
to cause something to be known publicly
to demonstrate that something is true
to take something from someone by means of deception or trickery
to cause someone not to possess something
senses.comment: Though the resulting state of ἀποστερέω[b] may be the mere absence of something, nevertheless the implication is that some activity has taken place to cause a person no longer to possess something. This meaning may then be expressed in some languages as to have something taken away from someone.

senses.def: to not pay someone for what is owed
pertaining to what is sufficient for some purpose and accordingly resulting in satisfaction
a state of having been without food, frequently with the implication of being caused by a lack of appetite

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being exacting, with a possible implication of being severe in either a favorable or unfavorable sense
pertaining to being considerably below a surface
an extreme point on a scale of extent

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of βαθύς[a] ‘deep,’ 81.10) the content of knowledge which is very difficult to know
glosses: secrets difficult to find out about
senses.comment: Only rarely can one use a literal rendering of τὰ βαθέα or τὰ βάθη in referring to secrets. In some instances it may be possible to use an expression such as ‘far away’ or ‘distant,’ and in other cases one can use expressions meaning ‘hard’ or ‘difficult.’ More often than not, however, the closest equivalent of τὰ βαθέα and τὰ βάθη in this type of context is either an expression of degree using a term such as ‘very’ (for example, ‘that which is very secret’) or an expression implying ‘that which is hidden’ or ‘that which is difficult to discover.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: pertaining to an extended period of time, with the implication of being slow to do something
the male role in causing the conception and birth of a child
to give birth to a child
senses.comment: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.|γεννάω also occurs together with ἐξ αἱμάτων (John 1:13) and ἐκ τῆς σαρκός (John 3:6) in reference to physical birth. In John 3:5, γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος has likewise been interpreted by some scholars as referring to physical birth (compare John 3:6), but others understand this as referring to baptism. Certainly the occurrence of γεννηθῇ with πνεύματος in John 3:5 is a reference to religious rebirth, in which case γεννάω would involve a radical change of state (see 13.56). The use of the same word with two different meanings or referents is typical of the style of the Gospel of John.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of γεννάω[b] ‘to give birth,’ 23.52) to cause to experience a radical change, with the implication of involvement of the total personality
senses.comment: The phrase γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος has been interpreted by some as a literal reference to physical birth (see 23.52). Others, however, interpret this phrase as referring to baptism by water. In a parallel fashion, the expression γεννηθῇ ἐξ … πνεύματος would refer to baptism by the Spirit or rebirth made possible by the Spirit.

senses.def: to cause to happen, with the implication of the result of existing circumstances
(an idiom, literally: to be born again) to experience a complete change in one’s way of life to what it should be, with the implication of return to a former state or relation
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἄνωθεν in John 3:3 as meaning ‘from above’ or ‘from God’ (see 84.13), a literary parallel to the phrase ἐκ θεοῦ ἐγεννήθησαν in John 1:13. In John 3:3, however, Nicodemus understood ἄνωθεν as meaning ‘again’ (see 67.55) and γεννάω as ‘physical birth’ (see 23.52).

senses.def: an evil supernatural being or spirit
senses.comment: While in a number of languages the Devil may be spoken of as ‘the chief of the demons,’ sometimes the demons are simply called ‘the spirits of the Devil’ or ‘the servants of the Devil.’|In a number of languages the difficulty in terminology for demons is not the absence of a term, but the abundance of different terms for different kinds of demons, each one of which may be responsible for particular kinds of human behavior, for example, insanity, depression, epilepsy, sex perversion, and violent assault. Sometimes demons are classified as ‘those of the home’ and ‘those of the forest,’ in which case the latter are normally regarded as more violent and virulent. When there is an abundance of different terms for demons and no generic term for all types of demons, one can usually select a class of demons which parallels most closely the descriptions of demon activity in the NT and use such a term with appropriate contextual qualifications so as to suggest that such a term is to be understood in a general sense.

senses.def: extension toward a goal at or near the speaker and implying movement
to signal to someone by means of part of the body, especially by means of the head or hands
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific with regard to types of gestures or motions of the head or hands and arms. For example, in John 13:24 there is an obvious question involved, and this may require in some languages a particular signal by means of the hands or face. The same would be true in the case of Luke 1:62. In Luke 1:22 the gesture would have to be something which would explain or indicate Zechariah’s inability to speak, while in Luke 5:7 quite another gesture would no doubt be called for, since the persons involved were at quite a distance from one another.

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to having existed for two years
senses.comment: This expression in Matthew 2:16 may be rendered in some languages as ‘children who were two years old and those who were not yet two years old.’

senses.def: to speak of something as being unusually fine and deserving honor

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: to attribute high status to someone by honoring

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: to cause someone to have glorious greatness
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of this expression in John 17:5 may be ‘raise me up high’ or ‘give me great glory in the eyes of.’

senses.def: to be of exceptional value, with the implication of being particularly praiseworthy
to come back to life after having once died
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a difficulty involved in formulating some expression for ‘resurrection’ or ‘living again,’ since such a phrase may refer to what is technically known as metempsychosis, that is to say, the rebirth of the soul in another existence, a belief which is widely held in a number of areas of south Asia. This problem may be avoided in some languages by speaking of ‘his body will live again’ or ‘his body will come back to life’ or ‘he will be the same person when he lives again.’

senses.def: to invite a person in as a guest
(figurative extension of meaning of ἐκμυκτηρίζω ‘to turn up the nose at,’ not occurring in the NT) to ridicule in a sneering and contemptuous way
to give to those in need as an act of mercy
(semantic derivative of ἐλεημοσύνη[a] ‘giving to the needy,’ 57.111) that which is given to help the needy
senses.comment: In some languages the closest equivalent of ἐλεημοσύνη in Acts 3:2 is simply ‘money.’

senses.def: pertaining to being extremely afraid
to give definite orders, implying authority or official sanction
to break something loose, usually by digging out and opening up an area

senses.subdomain: Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention
senses.def: to be in a continuous state of readiness to learn of any future danger, need, or error, and to respond appropriately
glosses: to keep on the lookout for
to be on one’s guard against

senses.def: to hold firmly to a particular belief
senses.comment: The equivalent of ἐπέχω[b] and προσέχω[c] may be simply ‘to continue to strongly believe’ or ‘to not give up at all to believe.’|It is also possible to understand ἐπέχω in Philippians 2:16 as meaning ‘to offer.’

senses.def: to direct one’s attention to a particular object or event
to stay or remain in a place beyond some point of time
longing for something, with the implication of recognizing a lack

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: seven occurrences
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἑπτάκις in Matthew and Luke as referring to a relatively large number, that is, more than one would expect from the context.

senses.def: sunny, mild weather without strong winds
senses.comment: Fair weather may be referred to by a number of different expressions, for example, ‘growing weather’ or ‘cloudless skies’ or ‘happy weather.’ The variety of expressions depends largely upon the type of activity associated with weather or the atmospheric conditions typical of what people regard as fair weather. In a number of languages fair weather is expressed as a negative of bad weather, that is to say, ‘a not stormy day’ or ‘a not windy day.’

senses.def: a state of joyful happiness
(derivative of ἡγέομαι[c] ‘to rule,’ 37.58) one who rules, with the implication of preeminent position
senses.comment: In the context of Matthew 2:6 it is possible to understand ‘rulers’ as a figurative reference to important places, and therefore one may also translate ‘you are by no means the least among the leading cities of Judah.’

senses.def: (the Greek equivalent of the Latin term praefectus) a person who ruled over a minor Roman province
a rather large, normally semicircular open structure capable of seating several thousand people and often used for public assemblies
senses.comment: The emphasis in Acts 19:29 is upon the theater as a place for assembly and not as a place for dramas. In some languages the most appropriate equivalent is actually ‘meeting place.’ In other instances one may use a term which designates an ‘enclosure.’

senses.def: (derivative of θεωρέω[a] ‘to observe,’ 24.14) an unusual object or event which is observed
(a diminutive derivative of θυγάτηρ[a] daughter, 10.46, with possible emphasis upon young age and probable implication of affection)
senses.comment: In Mark 5:23 the text indicates specifically that the daughter was twelve years of age, and it may very well be that in Mark 7:25 (the only other passage in which θυγάτριον occurs in the NT) the daughter may have been of approximately the same age. In languages in which some indication of relative age is obligatory, one could employ a term identifying a girl about the age of puberty.

senses.def: to forgive, with the focus upon the instrumentality or the means by which forgiveness is accomplished

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to show compassion and concern for someone in difficulty, despite that person's having committed a moral offense
senses.comment: In rendering ἱλάσκομι in Luke 18:13 it is inadequate simply to indicate an attitude on the part of God. Having mercy or showing compassion must involve some act of kindness or concern.

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to suffer ill-treatment
to cause someone to be much ashamed
to cause a shadow by interposing something between an object and a source of light
senses.comment: It is possible in Hebrews 9:5 to regard the action of the cherubim as being one of protection, but it is also possible to regard this as an expression of overshadowing in view of the position of the cherubim whose wings covered the top of the Covenant Box.

senses.def: to express an unusually high degree of confidence in someone or something being exceptionally noteworthy
senses.comment: Whether in any particular context the boasting is legitimate or not depends upon what is boasted about. In a number of languages, however, quite different terms are employed, depending upon the differing degrees of justification for such boasting.

senses.def: (derivative of καυχάομαι ‘to boast,’ 33.368) the referent of boasting, namely, that which one boasts about
senses.comment: For another interpretation of καύχημα in 2 Corinthians 1:14, see 25.203.

senses.def: the justification for boasting
the basis for or the content of one’s feeling of legitimate pride
senses.comment: For another interpretation of καύχημα in 2 Corinthians 1:14, see 33.371.

senses.def: to break an object into two or more parts (in the NT κλάω and κλάσις are used exclusively for breaking bread)
senses.comment: In some languages important distinctions are made for terms meaning ‘to break’ depending on the substance involved. For example, the breaking of a stick or a bone would require quite a different term from that used in speaking of breaking bread. Furthermore, the action of breaking bread would probably imply breaking into several pieces rather than a single break. Such a distinction may likewise require a special term.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to break bread) to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
senses.comment: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.|The implication of ‘eating together’ comes from the total context. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων συνηγμένων ἡμῶν κλάσαι ἄρτον ‘on the first day of the week we gathered together for a meal’ Acts 20:7. No doubt the reference in Acts 20:7 is to the ‘fellowship meal,’ called ‘agape,’ which constituted the early Christian form of the ‘Lord’s Supper.’ See 23.28.

senses.def: beating the breast and lamenting as an expression of sorrow
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is entirely impossible to use an expression such as ‘to beat the breast’ in referring to mourning or grief, since ‘to beat the breast’ is often employed as a gesture of self-congratulation or pride in accomplishment. In a number of instances the closest equivalent of ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to beat the head’ or even ‘to pull out the hair.’

senses.def: to acquire possession of something

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to acquire one’s soul, or: to acquire one’s life) to save oneself from grave danger or death
(an idiom, literally: to possess a vessel) a euphemistic manner of referring to sexual relations
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand σκεῦος in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 as one’s wife (see 10.55). σκεῦος in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 may also be understood as one’s body, and therefore the phrase τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι may be rendered as ‘to control his own body’ (see 8.6).

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the largest unit into which the people of the world are divided on the basis of their constituting a socio-political community
senses.comment: In a number of languages a term meaning basically ‘tribe’ has been extended in meaning to identify ‘nations.’ In other instances different nations are spoken of simply as ‘different peoples.’ In certain cases distinct nations are classified primarily in terms of their diverse languages, for example, ‘those people who speak different languages.’ Such an expression should not, however, be used if it only refers to multilingual persons.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a collective for people who belong to God (whether Jews or Christians)
senses.comment: The phrase ‘people of God’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘the people who belong to God’ or ‘the people whom God possesses,’ but in a number of languages the relationship between the people and God must be expressed in terms of reverence or worship, for example, ‘the people who worship God’ or ‘the people who reverence God.’ See also 11.27.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a casual non-membership group of people, fairly large in size and assembled for whatever purpose
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no term corresponding to ‘crowd.’ One may, however, usually speak of such a group of people as ‘many people’ or ‘many men and women.’ Depending on the context, it may be necessary to indicate some relative difference in size, for example, ‘very large crowd’ or ‘many, many people.’ If the crowd is relatively small, one may sometimes speak of ‘just some people.’

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: the common people, in contrast with those who are rich, leaders, and/or authorities in the society, often with the implication of disdain and low esteem
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘the common people’ is ‘the poor people,’ but in some languages an equivalent depends upon geographical location, for example, ‘those who live on the edge of town’ (the opposite situation from what exists in most present-day metropolitan centers). In still other languages ‘the common people’ may be designated in terms of lack of status, for example, ‘those who have no position’ or ‘those whom the rich do not greet’ or ‘those before whom no one ever bows.’

senses.def: that which has been stated or said, with primary focus upon the content of the communication
senses.comment: Any difference of meaning between λόγος[a] and ῥῆμα[b] would be only a matter of stylistic usage.|In Matthew 21:24 λόγος may be rendered as ‘question’ in view of the preceding ἐρωτάω[a] ‘to ask’ (33.180).

senses.def: the act of speaking
the content of what is preached about Christ or about the good news
a relatively formal and systematic treatment of a subject

a title for Jesus in the Gospel of John as a reference to the content of God’s revelation and as a verbal echo of the use of the verbs meaning ‘to speak’ in Genesis 1 and in many utterances of the prophets
a record of assets and liabilities
senses.comment: The phrase εἰς λόγον in Philippians 4:17 is a technical expression referring to the settlement of an account and indicates that this is a credit to the account. Accordingly, one may properly translate λόγον as ‘the amount of an account.’

senses.def: a reason, with the implication of some verbal formulation
a happening to which one may refer
that which is thought to be true but is not necessarily so
a formal declaration of charges against someone in court
(an idiom, literally: word runs) a message which becomes widely and rapidly known
glosses: for a message to spread rapidly

senses.subdomain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to make of reason) to have an opinion based on some reason
a state of emotional calm in the face of provocation or misfortune and without complaint or irritation
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘patience’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to remain seated in one’s heart’ or ‘to keep one’s heart from jumping’ or ‘to have a waiting heart.’

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause someone to change a place of habitation
a container for dry matter with a capacity of about eight liters (about two gallons)
senses.comment: A μόδιος is variously translated as ‘basket,’ ‘bucket,’ ‘box,’ and ‘bowl.’

senses.def: a larger ocean-going vessel used for transporting cargo and people
senses.comment: The term ναῦς occurs in the NT only in Acts 27:41, where it refers to the ship which was wrecked at Malta. See 6.42.

senses.def: the young of any bird
(derivative of οἰκοδομέω[a] ‘to build,’ 45.1) one who builds
senses.comment: Normally refers to builders of houses and other types of relatively large constructions.

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: a low status characterized by public disgrace
pertaining to a comparative quantity of objects or events
pertaining to a comparison of a quantity

senses.subdomain: Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]
senses.def: a degree of correlative extent
senses.comment: Expressions involving correspondence of degrees must often be rather considerably restructured. For example, in the first part of Revelation 18:7 one may translate in some languages ‘she honored herself very much and lived in great luxury, and so give her very much suffering and grief.’ In the case of Hebrews 1:4, one may translate ‘God gave his Son a name that was more important than the name of the angels; therefore, God’s Son is greater than the angels.’|One may also render this expression in Hebrews 8:6 as ‘Christ’s ministry is better than the old to the same degree that the covenant he mediates is better.’|In Romans 11:13 ὅσον is strengthened by ἐπί (see 78.51).

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time
senses.comment: The additon of ἐπί (degree, 78.51) and/or χρόνος (time, 67.78) reinforces this meaning of ὅσος.

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: the period from the time a person is a child until the time of the context
senses.comment: In παιδιόθεν, the stem παιδιο would suggest an age somewhat older than in the case of βρέφος[b] ‘infancy’ (67.152). παιδιόθεν, accordingly, would probably refer to a period of time which begins after a child has been weaned.

senses.def: to take or bring someone along with
to take or lead off to oneself
to acquire information from someone, implying the type of information passed on by tradition
to accept the presence of a person with friendliness

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: to receive an appointment for a particular ministry
to receive traditional instruction
a short saying in fixed form, emphasizing some general truth
senses.comment: In a context such as 2 Peter 2:22 one may render ‘saying’ as ‘what people so often say’ or ‘what is often said.’

senses.def: a relatively short narrative with symbolic meaning
senses.comment: In almost all languages there is some way of speaking about parables or allegories. The equivalent in some languages may be ‘a likeness story’ or ‘a story that teaches’ or ‘a story that points the way’ or ‘words that have another meaning’ or ‘words that are saying something else important.’|Some scholars have insisted that in the NT παραβολή is used only in the sense of a story with one level of symbolic meaning, but in some contexts παραβολή is also used to identify allegories in which each element of the account has a symbolic significance. It is therefore extremely difficult to make a rigid distinction between parables and allegories.

senses.def: a Jewish harvest festival celebrated on the fiftieth day after Passover
senses.comment: In most languages the festival of Pentecost is identified simply by a borrowed term based on the Greek expression πεντηκοστή. Some languages, however, use a phrase such as ‘the festival of the fiftieth day,’ and then in a footnote explain the fact that this was a harvest or thanksgiving festival occurring fifty days after Passover.

senses.def: to praise oneself excessively
a marker of contrast, implying the validity of something irrespective of other considerations
a marker of sets of items in contrast with one another
glosses: on the one hand … but on the other hand

senses.def: to move a considerable distance, either with a single destination or from one destination to another in a series
business pursuits, with the implication of extensive activity and journeys required
to speak in such a way as to encourage a particular type of behavior or action
senses.comment: It is also possible that προβιβάζω in Matthew 14:8 should be interpreted to mean ‘to be urged on beforehand’ or ‘to be put forward.’

senses.def: to urge a particular course of action
to dispose of property or provide services in exchange for money or other valuable considerations
senses.comment: πιπράσκω and ἀποδίδομαι (ἀποδίδωμι[e]) may also be used to refer to selling a person into slavery. Note, for example, πιπράσκω in Matthew 18:25 (ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος πραθῆναι ‘his master ordered him to be sold as a slave’) and ἀποδίδομαι in Acts 7:9 (οἱ πατριάρχαι ζηλώσαντες τὸν Ἰωσὴφ ἀπέδοντο εἰς Αἴγυπτον ‘the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph and sold him to be a slave in Egypt’).|In a number of languages, however, it may be important to use a distinctive term for selling a person into slavery. In fact, it may be necessary to describe the event rather explicitly, for example, ‘to receive money for handing a person over to someone else to be a slave.’|In Romans 7:14 πιπράσκω is used figuratively in the phrase πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ‘sold as a slave to sin,’ in the sense that sin is personified as the master.

senses.def: an Aramaic word meaning: you have forsaken me
senses.comment: Languages differ appreciably in expressions meaning ‘to forsake, to abandon.’ For example, the most appropriate equivalent in some instances is ‘to leave alone’ or ‘to leave behind.’ In other instances one may employ a phrase such as ‘to leave without help’ or ‘to leave and refuse to care for.’

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being obdurate and obstinate
senses.comment: In the contexts illustrated by σκληροτράχηλος, ἀπερίτμητος καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, and σκληροκαρδία, the focus of the stubbornness and obstinacy is the unwillingness to be taught or to understand.

senses.def: a measure of distance of about 600 feet or 185 meters
senses.comment: The stade is normally adapted to familiar measurements of distance.

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: a person who belongs to the same extended family or clan

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person who is a member of the same πατριά[b] or φυλή[b] ‘nation’ (11.56)
senses.comment: The term ἄνδρες is often added to ἀδελφοί[d], constituting a lexical unit having essentially the same meaning as ἀδελφοί[d], but with the connotation of greater formality: ἄνδρες ἀδελφοίἐξὸν εἰπεῖν μετὰ παρρησίας πρὸς ὑμᾶς ‘fellow countrymen, I can speak to you quite plainly’ Acts 2:29.|συμφυλέτης[d] may often be translated by a phrase, for example, ‘a person of the same country’ or ‘a man who belongs to the same nation’ or ‘one who is part of the same tribe.’

senses.def: the movement of two or more objects to the same location
senses.comment: In a number of languages important distinctions are made in terms referring to gathering or assembling of animate beings. The distinctions are usually based upon the number of individuals, the distance which they have come, and whether or not the individuals in question constitute a membership group or whether they are merely a loose aggregation. In view of these types of distinctions, it is likely that quite different terms will be required for the various contexts listed for this set of related meanings.

senses.def: to join in attacking
senses.comment: In Acts 24:9 συνεπιτίθεμαι does not involve physical force but strong verbal opposition. It may therefore be more appropriate to translate ‘they opposed him strongly with their words’ or ‘they spoke very strongly against him.’

senses.def: to form or mold one’s behavior in accordance with a particular pattern or set of standards
